paragraphs: In the last three numbers I surveyed the main circumstances and events that revealed the character and fate of other confederate governments. I shall now go on to list the most important of the defects that have so far disappointed our hopes in the system we ourselves have established. To judge soundly and safely what the remedy should be, we must be thoroughly acquainted with how far the disease extends and how malignant it is.

The next most glaring defect of the existing Confederation is its complete lack of any SANCTION for its laws. The United States, as now constituted, have no power to compel obedience to their resolutions or to punish disobedience, whether by fines, by suspending or stripping privileges, or by any other constitutional means. No authority to use force against delinquent members has been expressly delegated to them. If such a right were attributed to the federal head as following from the nature of the social compact among the States, it could only be by inference and construction, and in the teeth of the part of the second article that declares, "that each State shall retain every power, jurisdiction, and right, not EXPRESSLY delegated to the United States in Congress assembled." There is surely a striking absurdity in supposing that no such right exists. But we are left with a dilemma. We must either accept that supposition, preposterous as it seems, or contradict or explain away a provision that has lately been a constant theme of praise from the opponents of the new Constitution, and whose absence from that plan has drawn much plausible comment and harsh criticism. If we are unwilling to weaken the force of this applauded provision, we must conclude that the United States present the extraordinary spectacle of a government without even the shadow of constitutional power to enforce its own laws. The examples I have cited will show that on this point the American Confederacy stands apart from every other institution of a similar kind, and presents a new and unexampled phenomenon in the political world.

The absence of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another major imperfection in the federal plan. Nothing of this kind is declared in the articles that make it up. To imply a tacit guaranty from considerations of usefulness would be a still more flagrant departure from the clause I have mentioned than to imply a tacit power of coercion on the same grounds. The lack of a guaranty, though its consequences might endanger the Union, does not strike as directly at its existence as the lack of a constitutional sanction for its laws.

Without a guaranty, we must give up any help the Union could offer against the domestic dangers that may sometimes threaten the existence of the State constitutions. Usurpation may raise its head in any State and trample on the liberties of the people, while the national government could lawfully do nothing more than watch its encroachments with indignation and regret. A successful faction may build a tyranny on the ruins of order and law, and the Union could not constitutionally give any help to the friends and supporters of the government. The stormy situation from which Massachusetts has barely emerged shows that dangers of this kind are not merely theoretical. Who can say what the outcome of her recent convulsions might have been if the malcontents had been led by a Caesar or a Cromwell? Who can predict what effect a despotism established in Massachusetts would have on the liberties of New Hampshire or Rhode Island, of Connecticut or New York?

Excessive pride in the importance of the State has led some minds to object to the principle of a guaranty in the federal government, on the ground that it would be an officious interference in the domestic concerns of the members. A scruple of this kind would deprive us of one of the principal advantages we expect from union, and it can only come from misunderstanding the nature of the provision. It could be no obstacle to reforms of a State constitution made by a majority of the people in a lawful and peaceable way. That right would remain undiminished. The guaranty could only work against changes brought about by violence. For preventing calamities of this kind, we cannot provide too many checks. The peace of society and the stability of government depend entirely on how effective the precautions taken on this point are. Where the whole power of the government is in the hands of the people, there is less pretext for violent remedies for the partial or occasional disorders of the State. The natural cure for poor administration, in a popular or representative constitution, is a change of men. A guaranty by the national authority would be aimed as much against the usurpations of rulers as against the ferment and outrages of faction and sedition among the people.

The principle of fixing the States' contributions to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation. I have already pointed out how badly it fits the need to supply the nation's emergencies adequately, and the trial it has had has shown this plainly enough. I speak of it now only from the standpoint of equality among the States. Anyone who has studied the circumstances that produce and make up national wealth must be satisfied that there is no common standard or barometer by which its degree can be determined. Neither the value of lands nor the number of people, both of which have been proposed in turn as the rule for the States' contributions, has any claim to be a just measure. Compare the wealth of the United Netherlands with that of Russia or Germany, or even France. Then compare the total value of the lands and the total population of that small district with the total value of the lands and the total population of the immense regions of any of those three countries. We shall see at once that neither of these two measures bears any proportion to the relative wealth of those nations. A similar comparison among several of the American States would give a similar result. Set Virginia beside North Carolina, Pennsylvania beside Connecticut, or Maryland beside New Jersey, and we shall be convinced that the ability of these States to produce revenue has little or no relation to their relative holdings of land or their relative populations. The same point can be illustrated in the same way by comparing counties within a single State. No one acquainted with the State of New York will doubt that the active wealth of King's County stands in a much greater proportion to that of Montgomery than it would appear to do if we took either the total value of the lands or the total number of people as the measure!

The wealth of nations depends on an endless variety of causes: location, soil, climate, the nature of the products, the nature of the government, the character of the citizens, the degree of knowledge they possess, the state of commerce, of the arts, of industry. These circumstances, and many more that are too complex, too minute, or too accidental to list one by one, produce differences in the relative opulence and riches of different countries that are hardly conceivable. The plain consequence is that there can be no common measure of national wealth, and therefore no general or fixed rule by which a state's ability to pay taxes can be determined. The attempt to regulate the contributions of the members of a confederacy by any such rule is bound to produce glaring inequality and extreme oppression.

In America this inequality would by itself be enough to bring about the eventual destruction of the Union, if any way could be found to force compliance with its requisitions. The suffering States would not long agree to stay united on a principle that shares the public burdens so unequally, and that was bound to impoverish and oppress the citizens of some States, while those of others would hardly notice the small share of the weight they were asked to bear. Yet this is an evil that cannot be separated from the principle of quotas and requisitions.

There is no way of steering clear of this problem except by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way. Imposts, excises, and in general all duties on articles of consumption may be compared to a fluid that will in time find its level with the means of paying them. In some degree, each citizen's contribution will be a matter of his own choice and can be adjusted to his resources. The rich may be extravagant, the poor can be frugal, and private oppression can always be avoided by a judicious choice of the objects suitable for such taxes. If duties on particular objects should create inequalities in some States, these will in all probability be offset by corresponding inequalities in other States from duties on other objects. In the course of time and events, a balance will be established everywhere, as far as that can be achieved in so complicated a subject. Or, if inequalities should still remain, they would not be so great, so uniform in their operation, or so odious in appearance as those that must arise from quotas on any scale that could possibly be devised.

A signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption is that by their own nature they carry a safeguard against excess. They set their own limit, which cannot be passed without defeating the very purpose, which is to increase the revenue. Applied to this subject, the saying is as true as it is witty that "in political arithmetic, two and two do not always make four." If duties are too high, they reduce consumption, people evade the collection, and the yield to the treasury is smaller than when the duties are kept within proper and moderate bounds. This forms a complete barrier against any serious oppression of the citizens by taxes of this class, and is itself a natural limit on the power to impose them.

Taxes of this kind usually fall under the name of indirect taxes, and for a long time they must make up the chief part of the revenue raised in this country. Direct taxes, which relate mainly to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. Either the value of land or the number of the people may serve as the standard. The condition of agriculture and the size of a country's population have been regarded as closely connected. And as a rule for the purpose intended, numbers deserve the preference for their simplicity and certainty. In every country, getting a valuation of the land is a herculean task. In a country only partly settled and still improving, the difficulties grow almost to the point of impossibility. The cost of an accurate valuation is, in all situations, a formidable objection. In a branch of taxation where the nature of things sets no limits to the government's discretion, establishing a fixed rule that does not conflict with the purpose may bring fewer drawbacks than leaving that discretion wholly unrestrained.
